title: Why You Can't Hear an Owl Until It's 3 Feet Away 🦉
description:
How do owls fly without making a sound? Comb-like serrations on the wing's leading edge, a soft trailing-edge fringe and velvety feathers break up and hush the air swirls that make most birds' wings whoosh, so a barn owl's flight stays quiet in the range a mouse can hear.

topic: How do owls fly without making a sound?
script: Why can't you hear an owl until it's three feet from you? Most birds' wings churn the air into big swirls, and those swirls are the whoosh you hear. But an owl's front wing feathers have a comb, tiny teeth along the edge. They split the air into small, quiet streams. Then a soft, ragged fringe on the back edge and a velvety coat on top hush whatever noise is left. Big wings help too. A barn owl can fly as slowly as two miles an hour, and slower means quieter. Its wings mute the high sounds above sixteen hundred hertz, right where a mouse's hearing begins. So the mouse never hears it coming, but the owl hears the mouse just fine. If an owl flew over you tonight, do you think you'd hear it?
key_facts: Comb-like serrations on the leading edge of owl wing feathers break up turbulent air that makes a swooshing sound (Audubon)
A soft trailing-edge fringe and a velvety feather texture further dampen the noise (Audubon; Knowable/Smithsonian)
A barn owl's swoosh is below the threshold of human hearing until the owl is about three feet away (Knowable/Smithsonian)
Large wings relative to body mass let owls fly as slowly as about 2 mph for a barn owl (Audubon)
Owl wings mute frequencies above about 1,600 Hz, roughly where rodent hearing begins (Knowable/Smithsonian)
